blueprint_topic: Management of Care — communicable-disease reporting, jurisdiction-specific legal duties, and public-health communication
stem: A client is newly diagnosed with acute hepatitis B. Which nursing action is most appropriate regarding public-health reporting?

options.A: Follow facility policy and the applicable state or local reporting law so the case reaches the proper health department; acute hepatitis B is nationally notifiable.
options.B: Use the same direct CDC notification pathway in every jurisdiction because nationally notifiable status creates a uniform federal reporting process for health facilities.
options.C: Defer reporting until the health department first confirms that the case meets the national surveillance definition, then begin the facility reporting process.
options.D: Treat the report as optional unless the client authorizes release because sending an identified diagnosis to public health requires patient permission outside an outbreak.

rationale: A is correct. CDC distinguishes case reporting from case notification. Hospitals, health care providers, and laboratories report conditions to the appropriate local, state, or territorial health department according to applicable reporting law; who must report and the exact workflow vary by jurisdiction. Health departments then notify CDC about nationally notifiable conditions through NNDSS. CDC lists acute hepatitis B as nationally notifiable and states that acute hepatitis B cases should be reported to health departments as specified by state, territorial, or local regulations. B is incorrect because nationally notifiable status does not create one uniform direct-to-CDC reporting pathway for health facilities in every jurisdiction. C is incorrect because case reporting to the health department is the upstream process that supplies information for public-health case classification and national notification; it is not universally deferred until the health department has already classified the case. D is incorrect because when a condition is legally reportable in a jurisdiction, mandatory public-health reporting is governed by law rather than optional client authorization; HHS states that HIPAA permits disclosures required by law and that a provider does not need patient permission before notifying public-health authorities of a reportable disease.
educational_objective: Differentiate jurisdictional case reporting from national case notification: follow the applicable state/local law and facility process for acute hepatitis B while recognizing that the condition is nationally notifiable to CDC through public-health surveillance systems.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights (HHS/OCR)
source_document_title: Hepatitis B Surveillance Guidance; General Surveillance; How We Conduct Case Surveillance; What is Case Surveillance?; Public Health Uses and Disclosures
source_version_date: CDC Hepatitis B Surveillance Guidance dated March 12, 2024; NNDSS How We Conduct Case Surveillance dated January 12, 2026; What is Case Surveillance dated March 25, 2026; HHS/OCR public-health disclosure guidance current and rechecked 2026-08-20
source_locator: CDC Hepatitis B Surveillance Guidance — 'Case Reporting /and National Notification': acute, chronic, and perinatal hepatitis B are nationally notifiable and cases should be reported to health departments as specified by state, territorial, or local regulations; 'Case Ascertainment': rules requiring facilities/providers to report hepatitis B vary by jurisdiction. CDC General Surveillance — overview and Table 1-1/Table 1-2: each state/territory mandates which diseases are reported to health departments; acute hepatitis B has national notification criteria and NNDSS event code 10100. CDC NNDSS 'How We Conduct Case Surveillance' — Case surveillance process: case reporting by hospitals/providers/labs to health departments according to state disease-reporting laws is mandatory; case notification from health departments to CDC is a separate voluntary national process. CDC 'What is Case Surveillance?' — 'Reportable or notifiable: What's the Difference?': states/territories set local reporting laws while CDC/CSTE identify nationally notifiable conditions. HHS/OCR 'Public Health Uses and Disclosures' — FAQ 294: providers do not need patient permission before notifying public-health authorities of a reportable disease; HIPAA permits disclosures required by law. HHS/OCR 'Public Health' — 45 CFR 164.512(b): covered entities may disclose protected health information without authorization for specified public-health purposes.
source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports that acute hepatitis B is nationally notifiable, that reporting to health departments is governed by state/territorial/local law and varies by jurisdiction, and that health departments—not health facilities through one universal federal pathway—send national case notifications to CDC through NNDSS. HHS/OCR directly supports that patient authorization is not required when applicable law requires reportable-disease disclosure to public-health authorities.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the item to correct a legal/public-health overstatement in the source candidate. The key no longer claims acute hepatitis B is mandatorily reportable in every jurisdiction or that an individual nurse reports directly to CDC. A post-fetch adversarial reread replaced overly obvious distractors with realistic errors about a uniform federal pathway, public-health classification timing, and client authorization. A subsequent legal-source audit added HHS/OCR support for the authorization claim before finalization.

option_audit.A: Correct; it follows jurisdiction-specific reporting law/facility process and correctly identifies acute hepatitis B as nationally notifiable without inventing a universal direct-to-CDC workflow.
option_audit.B: Plausible federal-uniformity misconception; incorrect because case reporting pathways are determined by state/local law and health departments submit national notifications to CDC.
option_audit.C: Plausible surveillance-sequencing misconception; incorrect because reporting from facilities/providers/labs supplies the health department with the information used for case ascertainment/classification rather than universally beginning only after classification is complete.
option_audit.D: Plausible privacy/autonomy misconception; incorrect because legally mandated communicable-disease reporting is not made optional by client preference, and HHS/OCR permits required-by-law public-health disclosure without patient authorization.
